newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FOCUS - JCI seen stripping assets to buy Lonrho.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - JCI seen stripping assets to buy Lonrho.

text.p: South Africa's first black-controlled mining house, JCI Ltd, said on Thursday it had guaranteed funds to buy 26.8 percent of British conglomerate Lonrho Plc for some 2.5 billion rand ($552.4 million) but was exploring other ways of funding the purchase.

JCI said late on Wednesday that in terms of an agreement reached earlier, it had been granted call options on Anglo American Corp of South Africa, De Beers Consolidated Mines Ltd and The Southern Life Association's combined holdings of some 211.08 million Lonrho shares -- effectively a 26.8 percent stake.
"We have guaranteed facilities in place to fund the deal but are obviously with the time available considering all options," JCI spokesman Marc Gonsalves told Reuters.
The deal would enable Anglo American to meet a European Commission directive to reduce its stake in Lonrho to 9.99 percent to avoid controlling the world platinum industry.

Among the options JCI could consider was to sell or merge its unlisted Tavistock coal division with Lonrho and dispose of non-core assets such as a 9.8 percent stake in Anglo American Platinum Corp Ltd and an 8.7 percent stake in British precious metals firm Johnson Matthey Plc.
"The sale of Johnson Matthey and Amplats is inevitable, otherwise the EU will come down on them like a ton of bricks," BOE Natwest analyst Paul Brogan said.
A merger between Tavistock and Lonrho's Duiker Mining Ltd could create a coal company rivalling the biggest coal producers in South Africa.
Analysts said the Tavistock coal division could be worth about 15 percent of JCI's total market capitalisation, which presently stood at some five billion rand.
Gonsalves said JCI had said previously that it did not consider its non-core assets to be of strategic value.
"If they sell Johnson Matthey and their stake in Amplats, they would probably realise close to 1.5 billion rand.
"That would leave about a billion outstanding which they could possibly raise through combinations of other assets," said a Johannesburg analyst who asked not to be identified.
Anglo has been known to covet Lonrho's prized stake in Ghana's Ashanti Goldfields Co Ltd and said last week Lonrho had suggested swapping its 33.6 percent stake in Ashanti for Anglo's Lonrho shares.
But analysts said the latest developments meant Ashanti was slipping further away from Anglo American, although Anglo did well out of the deal by getting out of the EU quandary.
"Tiny Rowland might not be happy that Ashanti goes to Anglo and might respond particularly negatively to it like he has done in the past," the Johannesburg analyst said.
Rowland, the former Lonrho chief and the British company's largest private shareholder, has criticised the JCI/Lonrho merger talks and is vehemently opposed to Anglo gaining a stake in Ashanti.
On Thursday, Rowland was quoted in South Africa's Business report newspaper as saying the deal did not change the situation for Anglo.
"This deal is just from the left pocket to the right pocket and isn't a major change for Anglo," Rowland said.
Analysts said the Ashanti management, though espousing a policy of treating all shareholders equally, believed no-one would gain control of Ashanti.
"Their unofficial viewpoint is that no-one is going to get control of Ashanti Goldfields," said Barry Sergeant, another BOE Natwest analyst.
-- Johannesburg newsroom, +27-11 482-1003 ($ = 4.526 South African Rand)
